lesson_title: Rebuild the Speedometer: Limits and First Principles
hook_text: Your bus averaged 70 km/h — but what was it doing at THIS exact second? Answering that took mathematics three centuries.
clip_script: A bus covers 210 kilometres in three hours. Average speed: seventy. Simple — distance over time. Now the harder question: what did the speedometer show at one exact instant? An instant contains no distance and no time. Zero over zero. Undefined. So rebuild the reading from scratch. Average the speed over one minute around that instant: seventy-two. Over one second: closer. Over a tenth of a second: closer still. The tighter the window, the less the speed can wander inside it — the averages are funnelling onto ONE number. That number, the limit of average speeds as the window shrinks to nothing, IS the speedometer reading. Now aim the same trick at a curve. Average gradient between two points: rise over run. Slide the second point toward the first and watch the averages settle — on y equals x squared at x equals two, they read five, four comma five, four comma one, four comma nought one... landing on four. That landing is the derivative, and the recipe that produces it — first principles — is where every rule of calculus is born.
visual_style: A bus dashboard with a trembling speedometer needle, a stopwatch window visibly tightening around one instant, then a glowing parabola whose secant line swings into a locked tangent as the averages count down to 4.
mood: Curious, cinematic, the quiet thrill of an ancient riddle giving way.
pacing: Rolling open, rhythm tightening as the window shrinks, a clean stop the moment the tangent locks.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build the machine that measures change at a single instant.
